entry: Display that detects touch input from a user, typically with a finger or stylus. A touchscreen combines a touch panel, layered over an electronic visual display, so that the screen serves as both input and output. The display is often an LCD or [[OLED]] screen. Users tap, swipe or pinch to act directly on on-screen content rather than through a mouse or touchpad, and touchscreens are common in [[Smartphone|smartphones]], tablets, laptops, point-of-sale systems and automated teller machines (ATMs). Technologies include resistive, [[Capacitance|capacitive]], surface acoustic wave and optical methods, and capacitive screens are the most prevalent in modern devices. The first resistive touchscreen was developed by Sam Hurst in 1974 while at Elographics; the first finger-driven capacitive touchscreen was invented by E.A. Johnson in 1965 at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, United Kingdom.

City (pop., 2023: 514,819), prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and capital of the Occitania region in [[France|southern France]]. It lies on the River Garonne, 150 km from the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and 680 km from [[Paris]]. Toulouse is the center of the European aerospace industry, home to the headquarters of [[Airbus]], and hosts the CNES's Toulouse Space Centre, the largest national space centre in Europe. Founded by the Romans, the city was capital of the [[Visigothic Kingdom]] in the 5th century and of the province of Languedoc in the Late Middle Ages. The University of Toulouse, founded in 1229, is among the oldest in Europe. Toulouse has three [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]], including the Canal du Midi and the Basilica of St. Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe. Its pinkish terracotta architecture has earned it the nickname La Ville rose.

Burmese royal dynasty that ruled [[Myanmar|Burma]] from the mid-16th century to 1752. King Mingyi Nyo founded the First Toungoo Empire at Taungoo in 1510. His son [[Tabinshwehti]] unified most of Burma and was crowned king of all Burma in 1544. His successor [[Bayinnaung]] reigned for 30 years and conquered [[Manipur]] (1560) and [[Ayutthaya Kingdom|Ayutthaya]] (1564). At its peak the empire extended from [[Assam]] to the Cambodian frontier and [[Yunnan]]. It collapsed within 18 years of Bayinnaung's death in 1581. Nyaungyan Min and his son Anaukpetlun restored a smaller kingdom, based at Ava (Inwa), with a legal and administrative system that lasted into the 19th century. Palace rule, Meitei raids and a Mon rebellion weakened the kingdom, and in 1752 Mon armies captured Inwa and ended the dynasty.

Annual men's multiple-stage [[Cycling|road cycling]] race, held primarily in [[France]]. First organized in 1903 to boost sales of the newspaper L'Auto, it is the oldest and most prestigious of the three Grand Tours, along with the Giro d'Italia and the Vuelta a España. The race usually consists of 21 day-long stages over 23 or 24 days and covers about 3,500 km, with time trials and passages through the [[Pyrenees]] and the [[Alps]]. Since 1975 (except in 2024) it has finished on the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The rider with the lowest cumulative time wears the yellow jersey. Five riders, including [[Eddy Merckx]], hold the record with five overall victories each. Doping has marred the race, from [[Amphetamine|amphetamines]] in early decades to erythropoietin (EPO) later; [[Lance Armstrong]]'s seven titles, won from 1999 to 2005, were voided after evidence of blood doping emerged.

Neurodevelopmental disorder involving tics, which typically begin in childhood or adolescence. Tics are sudden, repetitive movements or sounds, often preceded by an unwanted premonitory urge. About 1% of school-age children and adolescents are estimated to have it; coprolalia, involuntary swearing, occurs only in a minority. There is no cure. Behavioral therapies are usually the first-line treatment, and medication is often unnecessary. [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|ADHD]] and [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|OCD]] often co-occur. The cause is believed to involve genetic and environmental factors and dysfunction in circuits linking the [[Basal ganglia]] with related brain structures.

Group of crystalline silicate minerals in which [[Boron|boron]] is combined with elements such as aluminum, iron, magnesium, sodium, lithium or potassium. The name derives from the Sinhalese *tōramalli*, a term for [[Carnelian|carnelian]]. Tourmaline occurs in a wide range of colors. Its most common species, schorl, is an iron-rich black mineral that may make up 95% or more of tourmaline in nature. Elbaite, a lithium-rich species, includes multicolored gems such as watermelon tourmaline. Major deposits lie in [[Brazil]], [[Madagascar]], [[Afghanistan]] and the United States. Its piezoelectric and pyroelectric properties are used in pressure gauges and electronics.

Haitian general and revolutionary, the principal leader of the [[Haitian Revolution]]. Born into slavery in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, he was freed before the [[French Revolution]], became a plantation owner and joined the 1791 slave revolt under Georges Biassou. He allied first with Spain and then with the French Republic, which abolished slavery, and gradually gained control of the whole island. In 1801 he promulgated a constitution naming him Governor-General for Life, challenging [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]]'s authority. Lured to a parley in 1802, he was arrested, deported to France and jailed at the Fort de Joux, where he died. His lieutenant Jean-Jacques Dessalines completed the revolution, and Saint-Domingue declared independence as [[Haiti]] on 1 January 1804. President [[Abraham Lincoln]] officially recognized Haiti in 1862.

Tall structure, taller than it is wide, built to serve purposes other than habitation. Towers are distinguished from masts by their lack of guy-wires and, like tall buildings, are self-supporting. Height serves functions such as clock visibility, surveillance from a [[Castle|castle]], observation, leisure and telecommunications. The oldest known may be a circular stone tower in the walls of Neolithic Jericho (8000 BC). Ziggurats, such as the Sumerian [[Ziggurat of Ur]] built in the 3rd millennium BC, were among the earliest towers. The Chinese used towers as part of the [[Great Wall of China]] in 210 BC during the [[Qin dynasty]], and medieval fortified buildings made wide use of them. Modern examples include the [[Eiffel Tower]] in Paris, completed in 1889 as a temporary entrance arch for the World's Fair, and [[Cooling tower|cooling towers]] at industrial plants.

Bascule and suspension bridge over the [[River Thames|River Thames]] in [[London|London]], England, close to the [[Tower of London]]. Built between 1886 and 1894 to designs by Horace Jones, with John Wolfe Barry as engineer, it was intended to connect the 39% of London's population that lived east of [[London Bridge]] and to let shipping reach the Pool of London. Its two 213-foot (65 m) towers are linked by high-level walkways, and a central pair of bascules opens to allow ships through. The bridge was opened on 30 June 1894 by [[Edward VII|Edward, Prince of Wales]]. It carries 40,000 crossings every day and is part of the London Inner Ring Road. It is sometimes confused with London Bridge, about 800 m upstream, which has given rise to an urban legend about an American buying the wrong bridge.

Tall building of many stories, used as apartments, offices or hotels, as opposed to a low-rise building. High-rise buildings became possible with the invention of the [[Elevator|elevator]] and with cheaper, more abundant materials. Most North American-style [[Skyscraper|skyscrapers]] have a [[Steel|steel]] frame, while residential blocks are usually built of [[Concrete|concrete]]. High-rise apartment buildings existed in [[Ancient Rome]], where insulae possibly reached ten or more stories. Roman emperors, beginning with [[Augustus]], set height limits of 20–25 metres, but these were often ignored. The 1968 Ronan Point partial collapse and the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire, which killed 72 people, exposed construction and cladding flaws. Apartment blocks accommodate more inhabitants per unit of land than houses and are common in densely populated cities worldwide.

Origin myth in the [[Book of Genesis]] explaining the existence of different languages. In the story, a united humanity speaking one language migrates to Shinar in lower [[Mesopotamia]] and builds a city with a tower meant to reach the sky. [[Yahweh]] confuses their speech and scatters them across the earth.Modern scholars often link the tale to Etemenanki, a ziggurat dedicated to the god Marduk in [[Babylon|Babylon]], which was called Babel in Hebrew. The name Babel is linked to a Hebrew verb meaning "to confuse", and the phrase "Tower of Babel" does not appear in the Bible.

Historic citadel and castle on the north bank of the [[River Thames|River Thames]] in London, England. Founded toward the end of 1066 as part of the [[Norman Conquest]], its White Tower was built by [[William the Conqueror]] in 1078. Set within two concentric walls and a [[Moat|moat]], it has served as a royal residence, armory and treasury, and holds the Crown Jewels. It also held prisoners such as [[Elizabeth I|Elizabeth I]] before she became queen. Only seven people were executed within it before the world wars of the 20th century. It is a [[World Heritage Site]].

Degree to which a chemical substance or mixture can damage an organism, whether a whole animal, bacterium or plant, a [[Cell (biology)|cell]] or an organ such as the [[Liver|liver]]. Toxicity is dose-dependent: even water can cause intoxication in too high a dose, whereas a very toxic substance such as [[Venom|snake venom]] has a dose below which no toxic effect is detectable. Toxicity is species-specific, which complicates cross-species analysis. The word derives from the Greek *toxon*, "arc", in reference to poisoned arrows. Toxicity is generally classified as chemical, biological, physical, radioactive or behavioral. Biological toxicants include [[Pathogen|pathogens]] and the toxins of microorganisms, plants and fungi. Physical toxicants, such as asbestos fibers and coal dust, can be fatal when inhaled.

Scientific discipline, overlapping with [[Biology|biology]], [[Chemistry|chemistry]], [[Pharmacology|pharmacology]] and [[Medicine|medicine]], that studies the adverse effects of chemical substances on living organisms. It also covers diagnosing and treating exposure to toxins and toxicants. The relationship between dose and effect is central, and factors include dosage, duration of exposure, route, species, age, sex and environment. Egyptian records of poisons date only to about 300 BC. [[Maimonides]] wrote a treatise on poisons and their treatment in the 12th century. The 16th-century Swiss physician [[Paracelsus]] is considered the father of modern toxicology. The field now contributes to [[Cancer|cancer]] research, since some toxins can be used as drugs to kill tumor cells, such as ribosome-inactivating proteins tested in the treatment of [[Leukemia|leukemia]].

Parasitic disease caused by the [[Protozoa|protozoan]] *Toxoplasma gondii*. Infection is usually spread by eating poorly cooked food containing cysts, by exposure to infected [[Cat|cat]] [[Feces|feces]], or from mother to baby during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. Up to half the world's population is infected, usually without symptoms. Most infections cause no symptoms or only mild, flu-like illness. In people with weakened [[Immune system|immune systems]], severe symptoms such as seizures can occur, and congenital infection can harm the child. Treatment of healthy people is usually unnecessary, and prevention includes thoroughly cooking food and avoiding cat litter during pregnancy.

Computer-animated adventure comedy film (1995) directed by John Lasseter. It was the first entirely computer-animated feature film and the first feature produced by [[Pixar]] for Walt Disney Pictures. Set in a world where toys come to life, it follows a cowboy doll, Woody, voiced by [[Tom Hanks|Tom Hanks]], who becomes jealous of a space ranger [[Action figure|action figure]] named Buzz Lightyear, voiced by [[Tim Allen|Tim Allen]]. It set a record for the highest-grossing opening weekend and grossed over $363 million worldwide, making it the second highest-grossing film of 1995. It received three Academy Award nominations and was selected for preservation in the [[Library of Congress|National Film Registry]] in 2005. Its success launched a franchise, including *Toy Story 2* (1999) and the spin-off *Lightyear* (2022).

Japanese multinational automotive manufacturer headquartered in Toyota City, Aichi. The company was founded in 1937 as a spinoff of Toyota Industries, a machine maker started by Sakichi Toyoda. While still a department of Toyota Industries, it built its first passenger car, the Toyota AA, in 1936. The [[Toyota Corolla|Corolla]], developed in the 1960s, became the best-selling automobile of all time. Toyota was the first automobile manufacturer to produce more than 10 million vehicles a year, a record set in 2012. It pioneered mass-market hybrids with the Toyota Prius in 1997. Critics note that Toyota has been slow to adopt all-electric vehicles, focusing instead on hydrogen fuel cell vehicles such as the Mirai. It holds a 5.1% stake in [[Mazda|Mazda]] and is listed on the [[London Stock Exchange|London Stock Exchange]] and the [[New York Stock Exchange|New York Stock Exchange]].

Series of compact cars made by [[Toyota|Toyota]] since 1966. Since 1997 the Corolla has been the best-selling automobile nameplate of all time, surpassing the [[Volkswagen Beetle]]. Toyota reached the milestone of 50 million Corollas sold over twelve generations in 2021. Early models were mostly rear-wheel drive, and later ones are front-wheel drive. Production has taken place in Japan and at plants including [[Tianjin]], [[Karachi]] and [[Durban]]. Its traditional competitors have been the Nissan Sunny, the Honda Civic and the Mitsubishi Lancer. The name means "small crown" in Latin.

Japanese samurai and daimyō (feudal lord), regarded as the second Great Unifier of [[Japan|Japan]]. Born a peasant, he rose as a retainer of [[Oda Nobunaga]] and succeeded him after Nobunaga's death in 1582. He became the first commoner to hold the post of kampaku (imperial regent), then retired as taikō and remained the effective ruler. He conquered Shikoku in 1585 and Kyūshū in 1587, and completed the unification of Japan by winning the Siege of Odawara in 1590. His regime enforced social divisions, most notably through the 1588 sword hunt that disarmed peasants. He launched the Japanese invasions of [[Korea|Korea]] in 1592, which ended in a stalemate that damaged his prestige. His young heir, Toyotomi Hideyori, was displaced by [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] at the [[Battle of Sekigahara]] in 1600, leading to the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa shogunate]].

Vietnamese royal prince, statesman and military commander of the [[Trần dynasty|Trần dynasty]]. He commanded Đại Việt's armed forces when the [[Yuan dynasty|Yuan dynasty]] under [[Kublai Khan|Kublai Khan]] launched a second invasion in 1285, and he repelled two of the three major Mongol invasions. After early defeats and the loss of the capital Thăng Long, his forces drove the overextended Yuan army back to China. In 1288 a vastly outnumbered Đại Việt fleet ambushed the Mongol fleet on the Bạch Đằng River, almost destroying it. He used guerrilla warfare and scorched-earth tactics against the larger invasion of 1287. After his death he was deified as Đức Thánh Trần, and numerous places in Vietnam are named after him.

Vietnamese dynasty that ruled Đại Việt from 1225 to 1400. It was founded when Emperor Trần Thái Tông ascended the throne after his uncle Trần Thủ Độ orchestrated the overthrow of the Lý dynasty. The dynasty defeated three Mongol invasions, most notably at the Battle of Bạch Đằng River in 1288. Later succession crises and invasions from [[Champa|Champa]] weakened it. In 1400 Thiếu Đế, enthroned as a three-year-old, abdicated in favor of the minister Hồ Quý Ly. The Trần improved Chinese [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]], expanded south to defeat and vassalize Champa, and began using [[Paper money|paper money]]. The period was a golden age for the [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese language]], arts and culture, and the first Chữ Nôm literature was written then.

Lạc Việt sisters and military leaders of the 1st century AD, regarded as national heroines of [[Vietnam|Vietnam]]. Born to a wealthy aristocratic family in Jiaozhi, a [[Han dynasty|Han]] commandery in what is now northern Vietnam, they rose in revolt in AD 40 after the Chinese governor killed Trưng Trắc's husband. The rebellion spread across a broad area, and at its height the sisters and their allies controlled some sixty-five towns and settlements. Trưng Trắc was proclaimed queen regnant, the first female monarch of Vietnam. In AD 42 Emperor Guangwu of Han sent general Ma Yuan with 20,000 troops. The sisters were defeated a year later and either were executed or committed suicide.

American actress, singer and former adult film actress. Lords used forged identification to enter the adult film industry as a minor. After her true age was revealed in 1986, most of those films were withdrawn from U.S. distribution as [[Child pornography|child pornography]]. She then pursued mainstream acting, appearing in *Cry-Baby* (1990), *Blade* (1998) and *Excision* (2012), for which she won the Fangoria Chainsaw Award for Best Supporting Actress. She also appeared in the television series [[Roseanne|Roseanne]]. Her 2003 memoir *Traci Lords: Underneath It All* debuted at number 31 on the New York Times Best Seller list.

Sport of contests in running, jumping and throwing, also called athletics outside the United States. Foot-racing events, from sprints to long-distance runs and hurdling, are won by the fastest time, while jumping and throwing events are won by the greatest distance or height. Jumping events include the [[Long jump|long jump]], triple jump, [[High jump|high jump]] and pole vault, and throwing events include the shot put, javelin, discus and hammer. Combined events such as the [[Decathlon|decathlon]] test athletes across ten disciplines. Track and field is one of the oldest sports and was held at the [[Ancient Olympic Games]] in [[Greece]]. Its most prestigious competitions are the athletics at the [[Olympic Games]] and the World Athletics Championships.

Engineering vehicle designed to deliver high tractive effort at slow speeds, for hauling trailers or machinery. Most commonly it is a farm vehicle that provides power and traction for [[Agriculture|agricultural]] tasks, especially [[Tillage|tillage]]. Early powered farm implements were portable [[Steam engine|steam engines]], and the first gasoline-powered tractors were built in Illinois in 1889 by John Charter. [[Henry Ford]]'s mass-produced Fordson, introduced in 1917, made tractors affordable, and over 35,000 units sold in 1921 alone, and tractors enabled larger-scale farm operations in place of animal and human labor.Modern tractors have powerful engines, hydraulic systems and front power take-off (PTO) mechanisms. Roll-over protective structures and seat belts have become standard safety features.
